title: NASA's Webb Telescope Shows How Supernova Dust Chronicles a Star's Final Hours
excerpt: NASA's James Webb Space Telescope found evidence that layers inside the star that became Cassiopeia A merged just hours before it exploded 340 years ago.
content:
NASA's James Webb Space Telescope has revealed new details about the supernova remnant Cassiopeia A, known as Cas A, about 11,000 light-years from Earth. The remnant was created when a massive star exploded about 340 years ago.

The findings, announced by NASA on Nov. 23, 2026, and published in The Astrophysical Journal Letters, come from mapping the composition of solar-system-sized clumps of dust left behind by the explosion.

Webb found evidence of a "shell merger" — layers inside the original star mixed together shortly before it exploded, possibly just hours before its demise. Lead author Tea Temim, a research scientist at Columbia University, said: "Material within these shells churns and circulates, which can cause the shells to merge shortly before the supernova explosion." In this case, the oxygen- and carbon-burning shells merged, changing the star's structure significantly.

Webb's Mid-Infrared Instrument, known as MIRI, examined three regions: two inside the reverse-shocked region — one dominated by silica dust, the other by carbon dust — and the "Green Monster," a structure first discovered by Webb, found rich in complex magnesium silicates and made of material the star shed before it exploded.

NASA's retired Spitzer Space Telescope had identified the regions. Webb's higher resolution revealed the finer chemistry within them.

Why it matters

Supernova dust matters because it seeds new stars and planets. By showing how a star's layers mixed in its final hours, Webb is helping scientists understand how the dust that becomes part of future stars and planets is formed and distributed.
